faq: Do you write the code too?
Not in this service. You get the design, the OpenAPI file and a build plan. If you want us to build it, API Development is the matching service and uses this design as its starting point.
What do you need from me to begin?
A short description of who will call the API and what they need to do. Existing database notes, screens or partner requests help but are not required. We ask follow-up questions in writing.
Can you design around an API I already have?
Yes. Send the current docs or sample calls and we tidy the design, flag inconsistencies and suggest changes that do not break existing users. We confirm the scope before starting.
Which style do you use, REST or GraphQL?
REST with JSON is our default because it suits most small products. If your team already uses GraphQL or another style, tell us in the order form and we design to match it.
desc:
API design and specification for your product means planning every endpoint, data shape and error message before development starts. Ecom Swift LLC turns your idea into an OpenAPI file, a readable summary and example calls that any developer can build from.

## What is API design?

API design is the planning stage in which you decide what outsiders can ask your product to do. It defines the resources, the addresses, the request and response formats, the sign-in method and the error rules. The result is usually an OpenAPI file, which is a standard way to describe an API that tools and developers can read.

It happens on paper before it happens in code. That order matters, because changing a plan is cheap and changing a live API is not.

## Why design first

An API that grows without a plan ends up with inconsistent names, surprising behavior and endpoints that overlap. Once partners depend on it, every fix risks breaking someone's app. Developers then spend their days writing special cases instead of new features.

A design phase gives your team and your partners a single reference. Front-end and back-end developers can work at the same time, because both read the same file. Questions come up on paper, where they cost an hour, instead of in production, where they cost a release.

## What good design does for your product

A clear API makes your product easier to adopt. Partners can estimate the effort before they commit, and their first call works because the examples match reality. Support requests fall, because the error messages say what went wrong and how to fix it.

Good design also protects your future. Versioning rules let you add features without breaking older clients. Consistent paging and filtering keep large lists fast and predictable. The mechanism is simple: fewer surprises for developers means faster integrations and fewer fires for you.

## What a strong API design contains

- A list of resources named after your business objects, such as orders, customers and invoices.
- Endpoints with sensible verbs and predictable addresses.
- Request and response examples for every call.
- One error format used across the whole API.
- A chosen sign-in approach and the permissions that go with it.
- Rules for paging, filtering and sorting long lists.
- A versioning and change policy, so updates do not break existing users.
- A list of webhook events where your product needs to notify others.
- An OpenAPI file that tools can validate and turn into docs.

## How we work

We begin with a conversation about what your app, partners or customers need to do. You describe the tasks, and we turn them into resources and endpoints. Then we draft the shapes of the data and review the first version with you, adjusting names and rules until they match how your business talks.

The deliverables are the OpenAPI file, a plain-language summary and example calls. In larger packages we also add a review call with your developers, a mock API that returns sample answers so the front end can start early, and a build plan split into milestones. We design the plan; the code is a separate job unless you ask for it.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Name endpoints after things, not after screens.
- Use the same field names everywhere.
- Describe every error with a code and a message.
- Plan for versions from the first release.
- Let a developer who did not write the design read it before approval.

**Avoid:**
- Exposing your database tables as they are.
- Mixing several naming styles in one API.
- Returning huge lists with no paging.
- Adding sign-in as an afterthought.
- Designing for one client app only when others will follow.

## Who it is for

A startup about to hire developers needs a design to brief them and to compare quotes fairly. A company preparing to open a partner API needs a document that outsiders can read and trust. A team with a messy existing API may want a cleaner design to migrate toward step by step.

## How to get started

Send a short description of your product, who will call the API and what they need to do. Share any existing documents, screens or an older API if one exists. We work from what you provide, and no access to your systems is needed for a design job. If we do need to look at an existing API, we ask for a read-only developer user and never for passwords.
